You totally missed his point.

Hacking passwords takes advantage of human psychology. People tend to pick the same words when asked to pick random words. So for instance some of the most common passwords are for whatever reason shadow, pussy, and dragon. Then you consider common derivatives of these words you'd like to explore and this gives you a basic brute forcing list. There's not a single effective attack out there that's going to be pounding on troubador derivatives.

Suggesting people come up with passwords by choosing 4 random words is begging for super weak passwords that feeds into this exact psychological mechanism. You'll end up with a tiny number of words being repeated with an incredibly high frequency. Just hit on the top 64 words and you'd end up breaking a decent chunk of all passwords using this method. What would the complexity be? There would be 2^6 choices per word for 64 words. That's a total combinatoric space of 2^24 for 4 words. Using their method of 1000 guesses per second, those accounts are getting hacked in about 3 hours. Just hit the top 32 words, which would still again hack a good chunk of accounts, and your space is 2^20 which gets hacked in about 17 minutes.

Basically the 'secret' to a good password is simply to pick a password very few people would pick. Asking people to pick 4 random words is a terrible idea on this account because many of us are going to tend to pick the same words with an incredibly high frequency.

Using statistical methods is quite literally the type of cracking that we don't call brute force.

Brute force is systemically trying all combinations, dictionary attacks use combinations of words and letters from a "dictionary" source.

Wrong. Exhaustive search is used for absolutely nothing. Even this ridiculously inaccurate comic acknowledges this much. For instance if you were trying to simply brute force everything let's say by everything you mean A-Z, a-z, 0-9, !-). That's 62 characters. Let's round it up to 64 to make the math work cleanly. 64 is 2^6. That would be 6 bits of randomness per character. The proffered password is 11 characters long. That would be 66 bits of entropy, or about 2.3 billion years to crack at 1000 guesses/second. And that's "just" if you know the exact length of the password. In reality you'd also need to then add the complexity of all possibly 10 character passwords, all possible 9 character passwords, and so on. Not to mention going the other direction to whatever max length you want.

Brute forcing simply means repeatedly attempting to guess a password. There are no requirements of exhaustiveness. Nobody and nothing attempts to exhaustively try all combinations.
